Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:28: He explains the matter of the blemish, saying: "they act, so that the blessings from above are not drawn down upon them, as in 'and He will restrain the heavens, and there will be no rain.'" The intent is that it is the way of the supernal heavens to bestow good flow and mercy upon the lower beings, and the Holy One, blessed be He, must restrain them from bestowing in their usual way - as it is written, "and He will restrain the heavens" - and from this a certain blemish comes upon "the heavens," in the manner explained in the Zohar (Balak 197a), on the verse (Song of Songs 1:8), "if you do not know, O fairest among women" - that Malchut is called "Atzeret" [restraint], for she gathers in all the supernal flow that comes to her, and she restrains it, giving to the lower beings only drop by drop, because they are unworthy. In these words, in brief: "and when it reaches her, all that she has gathered, she restrains, withholds, and delays, so that it comes down only like dew, drop by drop. Why? Because she does not find faith below as she finds above, [where] it is poured out on every side without delay, and she rejoices, and then they give her many gifts and bounties, one upon another, and they do not delay her at all. But the lower beings delay them, and delay her, and then she is 'Atzeret,' restrained, held back; certainly, as it were, she gives [only] a residue, and no more" - to the extent relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:29: In this manner a blemish reaches "the heavens," in that they must be restrained against their own way, and from this distress comes to them - like the parable of a generous, open-handed man: if his hand is held back from giving, distress undoubtedly comes to him. "And they do not act" - "for the heavens take for themselves" - meaning that they are full of flow and blessing for their own needs, and the complete blemish that reaches the lower beings is that they receive nothing at all; this is [the meaning of] "and they do not take to draw it down below" - certainly, "the blemish is theirs," the wicked - and this is what they themselves caused.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:30: Further, "lo" spelled with a Vav [indicating] that the right is not comprised within the left - now he explains a further blemish that reaches above, in a manner different from what was said, saying that the right is not comprised within the left, so that the right should not be included with the left to subdue judgment, because the lower beings separate the evil inclination from the good inclination. And he said, "so that blessings are not drawn down to the lower beings" - returning to the first explanation, for the two matters are one; and therefore he did not say "another interpretation" but "further" - meaning an additional point beyond what was said, yet both are [essentially] the same.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:31: Now that a person knows that his situation is not like that of the other nations, the seventy nations - for whom, whether the good inclination prevails over the evil inclination or the reverse, their situation makes no difference [above], since they did not accept the whole Torah - but Israel, who are called children to the Omnipresent and are called "Adam," as it is said (Ezekiel 34:31), "you are Adam," and were created in the supernal image, as it is said (Genesis 9:6), "in the image of God He made man" - whatever they do affects the supernal roots, from the aspect of the soul within them, and the good inclination and evil inclination flow into them from above, as is explained in the Zohar (Bereshit 49a) - that they are the secret of the two arms, see there; and further there (ibid.), on the verse (Genesis 3:6), "and the woman saw that the tree was good for food." Therefore one must always fear lest he blemish himself - that is, his soul - through the removal of the supernal light from it; and this is [the meaning of] "his children, their blemish." For even though one might interpret "and He will restrain the heavens, and there will be no rain" as referring to physical rain - this would fit in years of famine, but if one sins in years of plenty, how would "and He will restrain the heavens" be fulfilled? Rather, it certainly refers to the withholding of the light of Torah from the souls below - for the Torah is compared to rain, as it is said (Deuteronomy 32:2), "my teaching shall drip as the rain," and so on, as our Sages, of blessed memory, explained (Ta'anit 7a); and likewise in the Tikkunim, "there is no rain except the flow of Torah."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:32: Thus one must fear lest he cause a blemish above, as I have explained, and therefore must always strengthen the good inclination over the evil inclination. And besides this, one must strengthen the side of kindness and mercy over judgment, such as the qualities of compassion, acts of loving-kindness, and the like - all of which flow from the good inclination, which is the side of kindness - and remove from his heart the qualities of cruelty, vengeance, anger, and envy, all of which are qualities flowing from the evil inclination, whose root is the root of judgment.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:33: The way for a person to acquire fear in his heart is to subdue the husks [kelipot] and strengthen the good inclination over the evil inclination; and this Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, taught us in the verse (Deuteronomy 10:12), "and now, Israel, what does the LORD your God ask of you, but to fear," where he said (ibid. 10:16), "and you shall circumcise the foreskin of your heart" - and it is known that the foreskin derives from the evil inclination; and since he called it "foreskin," we understand that the evil inclination has the laws of "orlah" [the foreskin of fruit, forbidden for three years] applied to it - "for three years it shall be forbidden [foreskinned] to you" - and it is explained in the Tikkunim (10b) that these three years correspond to the three shells of the walnut.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:34: And it is known that to eat the kernel of the walnut one must break the shells; therefore the prophets outside the Land, before reaching holiness, had to break through the shell: (Ezekiel 1:4), "and I looked, and behold, a stormy wind came out of the north" - this is one; "a great cloud" - two; "and a fire flaring up" - three; "and a brightness was about it" - this is the fourth, thin shell that is eaten together with the walnut, and from within it the likeness of the four Chayot [living creatures], which are the four compartments found within the walnut.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:35: And likewise these three shells are mentioned in the words concerning Elijah, as it is said (I Kings 19:11), "and behold, the LORD passed by, and a great and strong wind rending mountains and breaking rocks in pieces before the LORD, but the LORD was not in the wind; and after the wind an earthquake, but the LORD was not in the earthquake; and after the earthquake a fire, but the LORD was not in the fire; and after the fire, a still, small voice." My teacher, peace be upon him, explained in Sefer HaPardes that although the husks [kelipot] number ten, their roots are three, corresponding to the three shells of the walnut mentioned. From this we learn that although the qualities of the evil inclination are many, their roots are three, being three shells upon the evil inclination in the heart - and yet they are [ultimately] one, as we shall explain.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:36: The first is pride, corresponding to "a great and strong wind" - and without doubt pride is the root of all evil qualities, as we shall elaborate, with God's help, in its own Gate. And so it is explained in the Tikkunim (69b), that the heart is like the walnut, which has shells and a foreskin, in these words: "and the coarseness of the heart, which rules over its own shells and is not broken - of it is said (Proverbs 16:5), 'every haughty heart is an abomination to the LORD,' and the Shechinah does not rest upon it; and from the side of the shells, people are called 'uncircumcised of heart'" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:37: The second, corresponding to the hard shell of the walnut, is a person's stiffness of neck; and therefore Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, said (Deuteronomy 10:16), "and you shall circumcise the foreskin of your heart, and stiffen your neck no more" - and this too is a quality flowing from pride.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:38: The third is a person's boiling over in anger and harsh speech, including inflaming himself with the fire of the [evil] inclination to commit a transgression - this corresponds to "a fire flaring up," and this too is a quality flowing from pride, namely "the coarseness of the heart which rules over its own shells" - for the coarseness of the heart has these three shells mentioned, all of which spring from it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:39: I heard from the honorable Rabbi Avraham HaLevi that the reason it says of these three, "not in the wind of the LORD, not in the earthquake of the LORD, not in the fire of the LORD," is that the Shechinah does not rest in these three; rather, "in the still, small voice - there the King comes." And so it is explained in the Tikkunim (3b). And it is likewise the way of the members of an earthly king's palace to speak in a hushed manner, and one whose words are spoken in a low voice follows the ways of humility, and undoubtedly cleaves to the King, as we shall write concerning humility, with God's help.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:40: This is the aspect of inner fear: that a person should always consider that he is before the King, and fear before Him, and not raise his voice before Him; and this is what is explained in the Tikkunim (ibid.), "'a still, small voice' - this is the Yud" - although it is expounded there for a different purpose, nevertheless, for our purposes, since we explained above that the secret of fear is the Yud, we may learn what is needed to acquire fear: that it should be in a still, small voice, and that one should keep far from the three shells of pride, which are "a great wind," "an earthquake," and "a fire."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:41: It may be that this is what King Solomon, peace be upon him, intended in saying (Proverbs 8:13), "the fear of the LORD is to hate evil; pride, and arrogance, and the evil way, and the perverse mouth, I hate." For in order to merit the fear of the LORD, which is the good hidden away, the kernel of the walnut, one must break and crush the foreskin, which is the evil, and distance himself from it so much that it becomes hated and loathsome for him to draw near it; and this is "to hate evil" - the husks and evil in general are these three: "pride, and arrogance, and the evil way," and so on, which are the three shells of the walnut I explained, being the root of evil.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:42: Now, a person merits to break these husks by separating himself from the pleasures of the world, all of which derive from the husks of the serpent's foreskin and the evil inclination; and this is [the meaning of] (Psalms 34:10), "fear the LORD, His holy ones, for those who fear Him lack nothing." And Ramban, peace be upon him, explained (Parashat Kedoshim) that every expression of holiness refers to a person's separation and restraint from the desires of the world, and the restraining of his speech and the like; and I shall cite his words, with God's help, in the matters that lead to humility, one of which is holiness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:43: Likewise one must be careful of every negative commandment in the Torah, for whoever breaches the fence of a negative commandment causes the evil serpent to enter within; and this is [the meaning of] "fearing God and turning away from evil" (Job 1:8). And so said King David, peace be upon him (Psalms 34:12-15), "come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the LORD. Who is the man who desires life, who loves days to see good? Keep your tongue from evil," and so on, "turn from evil and do good." And the reason he juxtaposed to fear "who is the man who desires life" is that the fear of the LORD is a source of life, as I explained above at the end of chapter two.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:44: The matter of "turn from evil and do good" is the fear that Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in the passage we cited above from Parashat Bereshit (7b), "because it is the Tree of Good and Evil - if a person merits, behold, good; if he does not merit, behold, evil." Therefore it says "turn from evil" - to distance oneself from evil to the utmost degree of distance; and so said King Solomon, peace be upon him (Proverbs 14:16), "a wise man fears and turns away from evil."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:45: The reason is as our Sages, of blessed memory, explained (Avot 4:2): "one commandment leads to another commandment, and one transgression leads to another transgression." The pious Rabbi Yosef Yaavetz explained, in his commentary on this Mishnah, that the commandments flow from the Tree of Life and are spiritual entities cleaving to Him, blessed be He; and one who performs a commandment cleaves to Him, blessed be He, and the more commandments he adds, the more cleaving he adds - so that one commandment leads to another commandment, and the reward of a commandment is [another] commandment, in the manner of "the sanctuary itself: when consecrated from below, it is consecrated from above" - this is the abbreviated sense of his intent. And this is [the meaning of] "if a person merits, behold, good" - for the good to which he cleaves becomes his portion; and if, Heaven forfend, he cleaves to evil, the evil becomes his portion, and he is destined to do many evil things. And so the pious one, of blessed memory, explained there concerning "and flees from transgression" - that he flees as one who sees before him a great bonfire of wood, from which he must distance himself by a bowshot. I found support for this explanation in the words of our Sages, of blessed memory, cited in the Yalkut (Mishlei, remez 959), on the verse (Proverbs 19:2), "also, without knowledge the soul is not good, and he who hurries with his feet sins" - in these words: "our Sages taught: one commandment leads to another commandment, and one transgression leads to another transgression; a person should not grieve over transgressions he committed unwittingly, but [understand] that a door has been opened for him to sin even willfully; and a person should not rejoice over a commandment that comes to his hand, but [understand] that many commandments are destined to come to his hand. Therefore, if a person sins unwittingly, of him it is said, 'and he who hurries with his feet sins'" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:46: This is the aspect of the fear of sin - that one should distance himself from sin and fear it, for sin is the evil, the turbidity and refuse of holiness, and is a term of deficiency, as in (I Kings 1:21), "I and my son Solomon will be [regarded as] sinners [chata'im]" - for the husks are deficient in the supernal light. For this reason one must fear that a door will be opened for him to further transgressions, for "one corresponding to the other God has made" (Ecclesiastes 7:14) - just as one who performs the commandments cleaves ever more to the supernal spirituality the more he performs, so too one who commits transgressions cleaves to transgressions, in such a way that from an unwitting act he comes to a willful one.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:47: As for the reason it says "if a person sins unwittingly, of him it is said, 'and he who hurries with his feet sins'" - our Sages, of blessed memory, said similarly at the end of the third chapter of Yoma (39a), on "do not defile yourselves through them, lest you become defiled through them" (Leviticus 11:43) [homiletically read without the Aleph, "ve-nitmetem" as "ve-nitamtem," you become dulled/stopped up]: "a person who defiles himself a little, they defile him a great deal." And the same applies to the matter of holiness, as they said there: a person who sanctifies himself a little, they sanctify him a great deal.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:48: The matter is this: the soul within a person and the matter of the Torah's commandments as they have become physical follow the same pattern. For the soul within the human body is constricted, similar to how the Holy One, blessed be He, constricted His Shechinah between the poles of the Ark - for above, the heavens and the heaven of heavens cannot contain Him, and yet, for the love of Israel and their benefit, He constricted His Shechinah there. So too the soul: above, before it was clothed in this world, it shines without limit, greater than the angels, since its emanation and hewing is from the Throne of Glory, as they say, "the souls are hewn from the Throne of Glory." And just as every level of the Throne is great compared to everything beneath it, as we explained in chapter two, so too the souls hewn from it - especially if it is a soul of Atzilut, which shines ever more and encompasses with its light everything beneath it. And we already know that the soul is likened to the Holy One, blessed be He: just as the Holy One, blessed be He, sees and is not seen, so too the souls, as our Sages, of blessed memory, explained (Berachot 10a). And so our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Pesachim 8a): to what are the souls of the righteous, before the Shechinah, compared? To candles before a torch. And with this we may understand what is said in the Zohar (Emor 103b), that the souls of the Patriarchs, and Moses and Aaron, Joseph and David, come to every single sukkah of Israel [on Sukkot] - and how is this conceivable, if not in the manner described? We find, then, that the soul, within this coarse human body, is constricted in a way that is not its natural manner.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:49: And in this same manner it happened with the Torah and the commandments: for every single commandment, above, is a supernal light cleaving to the Tree of Life, for a commandment is "the LORD," as is explained in the Tikkunim (131b) and Ra'aya Meheimna (Pinchas 228b). But through the sin of the first man, and likewise through the sin of the [golden] calf, the Torah and the commandments became physical, and a person now performs a physical commandment, such as wearing a tallit with tzitzit, or leather tefillin, and so on for the other commandments. My teacher, peace be upon him, elaborated on this discourse in many places.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:50: And so it is explained in the Tikkunim (4a) concerning the vowel-points - that below they appear small to us, while above they shine without limit, like the sun, which appears small to us but is many times larger than the earth. And likewise concerning the letters, it is explained in Parashat Acharei Mot (73a) that upon the thorn [tip] of the supernal Yud hang many worlds, in these words: "one thousand four hundred and fifty myriads of worlds all hang upon the thorn of the Alef," and the other worlds hang upon the body of the Alef itself - see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:51: We find, then, that when a person now performs the physical commandment, and it appears in his eyes a small thing, in the eyes of the Holy One, blessed be He, it is very great - for in performing the physical commandment he arouses its spiritual root above, and its spirituality above has no measure or limit; therefore they said, "they sanctify him a great deal," without measure.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:52: Similarly, it is explained in Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of Self-Reckoning, chapter 5), in these words: "let no good deed you do for His Name seem small in your eyes, even a word or a glance, for what is little from you is much before Him" - and likewise regarding transgressions. And the closest analogy for this is the movement of the sun over the earth: a measure of a cubit's movement corresponds to many miles' movement in the [celestial] sphere; and likewise the movement of a shadow on an astrolabe" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:53: With this we may understand why the Holy One, blessed be He, needs to reward a person by appointing over each commandment many thousands upon thousands of angels, as Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained (Zohar, Pekudei 244b-262b) concerning the holy Heichalot [Palaces]. The reason is that the supernal light of that commandment's spirituality shines forth through all those small chambers. And if you ask, would it not suffice for there to be a single angel? We answer: it is impossible for the supernal light to shine forth in a single angel, for then that angel would be found equal in stature to the spirituality of the commandment itself in its own place, and would itself be the commandment - and this is not the intent; rather, the light shines forth into vessels through which the soul may derive pleasure. Nevertheless, there is one principal angel in whom the primary light of the commandment resides, and beneath him many thousands who receive the remaining sparks of light.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:54: From this we come to understand the matter of impurity: for when a person transgresses a single commandment of our holy Torah, such as eating forbidden fat or blood and the like, this thing, below, is physical and appears to the transgressor a small matter; but above it is impurity without measure - for according to the spiritual ascent of the commandment [when fulfilled], so is the measure of the descent of impurity [when transgressed], through many angels of destruction. Therefore it is explained [in the Zohar] that many bundles of impure spirits seize hold of the soul, as it says regarding the chambers of impurity several times (see Miketz 200a), and likewise "many wardens of the law" (263b, 265a) - for the great impurity, which is the matter of that great judgment, must be divided among all those forces to judge the soul, so that it can receive its punishment through each and every one of them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:55: We find, then, in this a reason for a person to distance himself from evil, which is sin, and to fear lest it come to his hand even unwittingly, because of the disgrace of the sin and the impurity within it - and instead to cleave to the good, which is the good that endures forever and for all eternity, "that it may go well with you," for the world that is entirely good and the world that is entirely long [everlasting].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:1: This chapter will explain the ways of fear from the aspect of the blemish that reaches above, to the Shechinah, and [will discuss] distancing oneself from the enticements of the evil inclination and drawing near to the good.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:2: Our Sages, of blessed memory, said, cited in the Yalkut, Parashat Chukat (remez 768), on the verse (Numbers 21:34), "and the LORD said to Moses, fear him not" - in these words: "this is what Scripture says (Proverbs 28:14), 'happy is the man who fears always' - such is the quality of the righteous: even though the Holy One, blessed be He, reassures them, they do not cast off fear from themselves. And so of Jacob it is written (Genesis 32:8), 'and Jacob was greatly afraid' - why was he afraid? He said, perhaps I have become sullied in some way while with Laban; and it is written (Deuteronomy 23:15), 'and He shall see no unseemly thing among you, and turn away from you' - and the Holy One, blessed be He, left me [i.e., protected him]. Even Moses seized upon fear - why was he afraid? He said, perhaps Israel transgressed in the war against Sichon, or became sullied through transgression; He said to him, 'fear him not'" - to the extent relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:3: According to the plain sense that appears from this passage: "and He shall see no unseemly thing among you" means no defiling matter, that is, the stain of some sin; "and turn away from you" means that the Shechinah would depart from him. And what is meant by "why was he afraid" may be understood from what our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 4a): "Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi raised a contradiction: it is written (Genesis 28:15), 'and behold, I am with you, and I will keep you wherever you go,' yet it is written (32:8), 'and Jacob was greatly afraid' - he was afraid lest sin be caused" - and the explanation of "lest sin be caused" is the matter of "perhaps I have become sullied in some way while with Laban," and so on, as written.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:4: However, in the Zohar (Acharei Mot 75a-b) it is explained that "an unseemly thing" [ervat davar] refers to the Shechinah, in these words: "Rabbi Shimon opened [with the verse], 'for the LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp, to deliver you,' and so on (Deuteronomy 23:15) - 'for the LORD your God' - this is the Shechinah, who is found among Israel, and all the more so in exile, to shield them always from every side, and from all the other nations, idol worshippers, so that they should not destroy Israel; for it is taught, the wicked of Israel's [own nation] cannot harm them until Israel weaken the strength of the Shechinah before the great appointed [angelic] princes of the other nations - then the wicked of Israel are able to prevail over them and rule over them and decree upon them many evil decrees. And when they repent to receive her, she breaks the strength and power of all those great appointed princes, and breaks the strength and power of the wicked of Israel, and exacts full payment from them all. Therefore, 'and your camp shall be holy' - for a person must not defile himself with his sins and transgress the words of the Torah, for if he does so, they defile him, as it is written (Leviticus 11:43), 've-nitmetem bam' [without the Aleph, 've-nitamtem,' you become dulled] - and we have learned, two hundred forty-eight limbs are in the body, and they all become defiled when he becomes defiled - that is, when he intends to become defiled. Therefore, 'and your camp shall be holy' - what is 'your camp'? These are the limbs of the body. 'And He shall see no unseemly thing among you' - the nakedness/blemish of this matter [davar], as we have established; for if this happens, then certainly 'and turn away from you.' And therefore, 'the nakedness of your father's wife you shall not uncover' - why? Because it is written, 'it is your father's nakedness,' as we have established" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:5: We have learned: for three things Israel is delayed [from redemption] in exile - because they treat the Shechinah with contempt in exile, and turn their faces away from the Shechinah, and defile themselves before the Shechinah; and all of this we have established in our own teaching - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:6: Now, in general, four aspects of the matter of the blemish are mentioned in this passage. The first is that when Israel sins, they weaken the strength of the Shechinah before the seventy [heavenly] princes; and this is the Shechinah's complaint (Song of Songs 1:6), "they made me keeper of the vineyards" - these being the seventy princes - "but my own vineyard," which is Israel, "I have not kept." Therefore it says (Deuteronomy 23:15), "for the LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp, to deliver you and to give up your enemies before you," and so on; but when a person causes a blemish, she does not deliver, but rather, Heaven forfend, the opposite - of her it is said (ibid. 32:18), "you have forgotten the Rock who bore you," as our Sages, of blessed memory, explained, which I cited in chapter three.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:7: Similarly, Rashbi, of blessed memory, said (Vayetze 152b), on the verse (Proverbs 24:10), "if you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small [tzar koach-cha]" - in these words: "'if you faint' - if he lets his hands go slack from Torah; 'in the day of adversity, your strength is small' - what is 'tzar koach-cha'? [It may be read as] 'tzar koach Kah' [restricted is the power of Kah, i.e., the Name Yud-Heh] - for it [this power] is always at his right, and its protection is always over a person when he walks in the ways of the Torah, and then it pushes the evil away from him, so that it should not draw near him and should not be able to accuse him. But when a person strays from the ways of the Torah and lets his hands go slack from it, then 'the power of Kah is restricted,' because the evil, which is on the left, rules over the person and pushes this 'Kah' outward, until it is forced into a tight place" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:8: The second and third aspects concerning the blemish are "and your camp shall be holy" and "and He shall see no unseemly thing among you." The matter is this: when a person causes a blemish above, he darkens that light in the aspect of that limb with which he sinned, and mercy withdraws from there and judgment prevails; therefore that blemish must be discharged below - whether by afflicting him with suffering in his body or his wealth, or that darkness and judgment are kept in store to be discharged upon his soul, by its entering the fire of Gehinnom, where it will be refined and receive that entire judgment in the measure of what it blemished; and this is [the meaning of] (Leviticus 24:20), "as he has inflicted a blemish on a person, so shall it be inflicted on him" - and "a person" [adam] refers to the supernal Adam.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:9: Now, to arouse a person to repent, they defile him and place upon him a blemish corresponding to the nakedness and the blemish he inflicted upon the "matter" [davar], which is the Shechinah; and this is [the meaning of] "he shall not see [lo yera'eh]," meaning that the blemish and nakedness you inflicted upon the "matter" should not be visible upon your body, but rather "your camp shall be holy" - that all two hundred forty-eight of his limbs should be holy, meaning that they should all be unified as one, to the point that we could say of them all that they are together a single, holy limb.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:10: The matter is this: when a person causes a blemish even in a single limb, it is accounted as though he blemished the entire stature, for all two hundred forty-eight limbs are unified as one; therefore, even if he sinned with only a single limb, all two hundred forty-eight of his limbs are defiled. And this is what Rashbi, peace be upon him, said: "two hundred forty-eight limbs in a single body, and they all become defiled."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:11: With this we may understand, in a second way, what our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Yoma 39a): "a person who defiles himself a little, they defile him a great deal" - meaning that even though he sinned with only a single limb, they defile all two hundred forty-eight of his limbs a great deal. And likewise regarding "and your camp shall be holy": "one who sanctifies himself a little, they sanctify him a great deal" - for even though he sanctified only a single limb, all two hundred forty-eight limbs, which are "your camp" in the plural, are sanctified with supernal holiness - "holy" [kadosh] in the singular, as I explained - just as our Sages, of blessed memory, said (see Kiddushin 39b): whoever performs a commandment as it is stated merits life in the World to Come.
